summary: Save the Breadbasket is a browser game where players design a satellite mission to watch a real problem: drought in Central Anatolia, Türkiye's main wheat region, where groundwater is falling fast, Lake Tuz dries out in hot summers and sinkholes are opening in farm fields. Players choose a mission goal, up to three instruments modeled on NASA Earth missions (GRACE-FO, SMAP, Landsat, GPM), a spacecraft bus, solar panels, a radio, an orbit and a rocket. Live bars show budget, mass, power and data, and the rocket will not launch until every limit fits. One player can play alone, or a team of up to four can split the roles of Mission Manager, Spacecraft Engineer, Scientist and Operations Lead, and every role must sign off before launch. The game then simulates 2022–2026 with solar storms, instrument faults and budget cuts, including the record-dry year 2025, and scores the mission out of 100 with a reason for every point. It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into choices students can test, fail and retry, and connects them to real NASA Earth science. The game code, text and slides were generated with an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic); this is stated in the game and in the project details.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Save the Breadbasket is a one-page web game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a satellite mission to monitor drought in Central Anatolia, Türkiye, in five steps: (1) pick a goal: Drought Watch, Lake Tuz Monitor or Crop Health; (2) pick up to three instruments, each with its own mass, power, cost and data rate; (3) build the spacecraft: bus size, solar panels and radio; (4) choose an orbit (sun-synchronous, low or geostationary) and a rocket; (5) every role signs off and the mission launches.

HOW IT WORKS

Live bars track the budget, instrument mass against the bus limit, total mass against the rocket's capacity for the chosen orbit, power with a 20% safety margin, data against radio capacity, and mission life. Launch is blocked while any limit is exceeded, and the game says exactly why. Orbits change the trade-offs: a low orbit is cheaper to reach but re-enters after about 3 years and misses the 2025 drought; a geostationary orbit lasts long but blurs the data, and gravity instruments cannot work there. The simulation then flies 2022–2026 with random solar storms, instrument faults and budget cuts. Spare power, backup electronics and a budget reserve protect the mission. The score out of 100 combines science value for the chosen goal (40), budget reserve (20), power, mass and data margins (20), mission life (10) and team balance (10), and each part comes with a sentence explaining why. The game also lists what the mission could not see because an instrument was missing.

TEAM PLAY AND LEARNING

Up to four players share one screen and take the roles of Mission Manager, Spacecraft Engineer, Scientist and Operations Lead. Each role has its own wish (for example, the manager wants a $50M reserve and the scientist wants 70% coverage of the goal). The wishes pull against each other, so the team has to negotiate before everyone signs off. Tap-to-explain tips define orbit, payload, bus, power margin, downlink, groundwater, re-entry and other terms in plain words. Easy, Normal and Hard levels change the budget and how often surprises happen.

WHY IT MATTERS

Mission design trade-offs are usually abstract for students. Here every choice has a visible price and a consequence, and the mission is tied to a real problem: groundwater in the Konya Basin now falls 4–5 m a year and nearly 700 sinkholes have formed (Reuters, December 2025), Lake Tuz dried out completely in 2008 and 2016 (NASA Earth Observatory), and 2025 was the driest year in Central Anatolia in 61 years (Turkish State Meteorological Service). The end screen links each game instrument to the real NASA mission that measures the same thing: GRACE-FO, SMAP, Landsat and GPM.

HONESTY AND LIMITS

Spacecraft numbers are simplified game values for learning, not real specifications, and the game is not a scientific model. Year-by-year story events are simulated; lines marked ★ in the game are real-world facts with their source. No NASA logos, flags or mission patches are used. The only pictures are simple SVG drawings made by the game code; no AI image generator was used.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with SVG drawings and no external code libraries (Google Fonts for the typefaces). It runs in any browser, on phones and computers, with no install. It was tested with automated playthroughs (Node.js with jsdom) and headless Chrome screenshots. The 7-slide demo was made with Claude's slide tool.

USE OF AI

Team NOVA9 chose the challenge and the drought topic and directed the work. The game code, the in-game text, the scoring rules, the slide deck and this project description were generated with Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic. This is stated in the game's footer and on the slides.

NASA Earth Observatory: Turkey Experiences Intense Drought (2021)
GRACE-FO mission (NASA JPL): basis of the Gravity Twins instrument
SMAP mission (NASA JPL): basis of the Soil Moisture Radiometer
Landsat Science (NASA): basis of the Multispectral Camera
GPM mission (NASA): basis of the Rain Radar
projectRefs: Turkish State Meteorological Service (MGM): 2025 Climate Report (Central Anatolia rainfall, 2025 drought)
Reuters via Daily Sabah (Dec 2025): sinkholes and groundwater decline in the Konya Basin
Habertürk (2024): 604 registered sinkholes deeper than 1 m in Konya (used in the demo slides)
Claude by Anthropic: AI assistant that generated the game code, text, slides and this description

jsdom (open-source): used only for automated testing of the game
